UK PARROT BUYING ENQUIRIES

Cockatoos for UK homes

Crownwing welcomes enquiries about cockatoos as a group, while the exact species, individual stock, rearing history and services must be confirmed separately. A practical buying conversation should help you understand one bird's established routine and the demands that come with its species, rather than relying on a general reputation for affection.

Available by enquiry

Cockatoo Parrots are available through Crownwing. Individual birds change regularly. Contact us for current birds, photographs and prices.

Species photographs are not individual stock listings.

Ask which cockatoo is involved

Confirm the species and ask what is known about the bird's approximate age, background and identity. A galah, cockatiel and large white cockatoo differ in scale, noise and day-to-day setup; 'cockatoo' by itself is not enough information for a buying decision. Clarify which facts are documented and which are an informed estimate.

Ask how the individual spends a normal day, which foods it accepts, what handling it tolerates and how it responds when left to occupy itself. Find out about familiar calls and activities without expecting a guarantee of future quietness or cuddling. If hand-rearing matters to you, ask what is known about this bird's rearing and weaning rather than assuming a method.

Availability and a realistic match

Enquiries about cockatoos are welcome, but that is not confirmation that a specific species or individual is available now. Ask what bird, if any, can currently be discussed, and whether its species and background are known. If nothing suitable is available at present, clarify whether a later enquiry is appropriate rather than treating a broad category page as a live inventory.

Describe your household honestly: the room available, neighbours, daily schedule, experience with parrots, family members and other animals. Ask which aspects of the bird's known behaviour will affect that setting. A useful match conversation may expose a mismatch; do not proceed simply because a bird appears affectionate during a short visit.

Price, recurring costs and setup

Ask for the current price of the individual bird and a precise list of anything included. No group-wide price or package should be assumed. Work out the cost of suitable robust housing, replacement enrichment, food, cleaning supplies and ongoing care, with allowance for the bird's potentially long lifespan and changing needs.

Before making a commitment, prepare a safe exercise area and a practical plan for calls, dust, cleaning and destructive play. Ask what equipment the bird knows and whether its familiar diet can be continued during transition. Confirm payment, reservation and collection details directly, and give household members time to agree on responsibilities.

Handover and settling-in questions

Ask what routine and written information can accompany the bird, what foods it is used to and how it is transported. Establish who to contact with ordinary settling-in questions and what information is not known. Do not expect an immediate bond or assume that the bird's first-day behaviour predicts its long-term response.

Cockatoos benefit from a predictable transition that respects their boundaries. Plan quiet time as well as interaction, and decide in advance who will manage feeding, cleaning and enrichment. If your schedule depends on the bird being continuously held or quiet, discuss that expectation candidly before you enquire further.

Would a second cockatoo automatically keep the first company?

No pairing can be assumed to work. Birds may prefer distance, so consider individual compatibility, separate resources and a way to maintain safe separation before treating another bird as a social solution.

Can a cockatoo's crest tell me whether it wants to be handled?

A crest is one visible signal, not a complete reading of mood or consent. Consider the bird's overall posture and context, and allow it to decline contact rather than using one feature as an invitation.
